<hypothesis>
To definitively distinguish the simple M1 mechanism from M7 (which requires two substrate molecules to form the productive catS2 complex) and catalyst-dependent inhibition models (M13, M19, M2), we need an experiment with a very high catalyst concentration and a low substrate concentration. 
By setting [cat] = 0.20 and [S] = 0.2, we create a regime where the catalyst is in stoichiometric excess relative to the substrate.
- For M1 (Simple MM): The excess catalyst will rapidly bind almost all available substrate to form catS. The reaction will be very fast, exhibiting an initial rate roughly proportional to the high catalyst concentration, and will quickly reach full conversion.
- For M7 (Substrate activation): The excess catalyst will act as a "sink," sequestering the limited substrate into the inactive 1:1 catS complex. Because M7 requires a second free substrate molecule to bind catS and form the productive catS2 complex, the severe depletion of free S will throttle the reaction. The rate will be dramatically slower than predicted by M1.
- For M13 and M19 (Bimolecular catalyst deactivation): The extremely high catalyst concentration will trigger rapid bimolecular deactivation (e.g., 2cat -> inactive), causing the reaction to stall almost immediately before S is fully consumed.
- For M2 (Catalyst dimerization): The high [cat] will drive the equilibrium toward inactive cat2 dimers. The reaction will proceed to full conversion but at a significantly lower initial rate than M1.
This single experiment will force a massive divergence between M1 and M7, while simultaneously screening for catalyst-concentration-dependent effects.
</hypothesis>
